messages.content: 從一顆距離地球4光年的恆星發出的光需要多少時間才能抵達地球？

function.name: light_travel_time
function.description: Calculate the time taken for light to travel from a celestial body to another. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

distance_in_light_years.description: The distance between the two celestial bodies in light years.

speed_of_light.description: The speed of light in vacuum, in m/s. Default value is 299792458 m/s.

message.reasoning:
The user asks: "從一顆距離地球4光年的恆星發出的光需要多少時間才能抵達地球？" They want the time it takes for light to travel from a star 4 light-years away to Earth. That is simply 4 years. But we might need to use the function to calculate? The function calculates time given distance in light years and speed of light. But the distance is already in light years, so the time would be distance / (speed_of_light / c?) Wait, the function expects distance in light years, speed of light in m/s. It will compute time. But if distance is in light years, dividing by speed of light in m/s yields seconds? Actually, distance in light years is a unit of time: 1 light year is the distance light travels in one year. So if we input distance_in_light_years=4, speed_of_light default 299792458 m/s, the function will compute time in seconds? Let's check: If distance is 4 light years, then time = distance_in_light_years * (light year in meters) / speed_of_light. Light year in meters is speed_of_light * seconds per year. So time = distance_in_light_years * speed_of_light * seconds_per_year / speed_of_light = distance_in_light_years * seconds_per_year. So time in seconds = 4 * seconds_per_year. Then convert to years: 4 years. So the answer is 4 years.

We can call the function with distance_in_light_years=4. The function will return something. We should call it.
